# Ray-Volume and Bounding Box Intersection


## Overview
This family provides geometric methods to determine if a viewing ray intersects a volume's bounding region and to calculate the entry/exit intervals for subsequent sampling [G]. It solves the problem of early rejection, ensuring that rays missing the data volume are discarded before expensive traversal occurs [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The shared principles of this family are the geometric definition of rays and the parallel execution model [G].
**Ray Definition**
Rays are defined by an origin $\mathbf{o}$ and a direction $\mathbf{d}$ [G]. The direction is typically normalized. The origin is often the camera eye position, but can vary based on the camera model [G].
**Parallel Execution**
Computations are mapped to parallel threads [G]. Each thread typically processes one or more pixels or samples [G]. Memory access patterns are optimized for coalescing [G]. Synchronization is used to manage data dependencies between threads [G].

## Subtopics

### [Ray-box intersection](776-ray-box-intersection.md)
The Ray-box intersection method computes the parametric entry ($t_{near}$) and exit ($t_{far}$) distances where a ray intersects an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). It solves the problem of determining the valid sampling interval along a ray for volume rendering, enabling early rejection of rays that miss the volume entirely. It sets itself apart by exploiting axis-alignment to perform the test analytically with minimal arithmetic operations. Choose it when rendering axis-aligned volumes for maximum performance [G].

### [Ray-Volume Intersection (Face Distance Method)](2381-ray-volume-intersection-face-distance-method.md)
This method determines if a viewing ray intersects the bounding volume of a dataset and calculates the entry point for subsequent volume traversal. It serves as the initial geometric culling step in ray casting, ensuring that rays missing the data volume are discarded before expensive sampling occurs. It sets itself apart by explicitly computing distances to the six faces of the data volume to determine a planar impact coordinate rather than using slab intervals. Choose it when volume boundaries are defined by explicit planar faces [G].

### [Ray Filtering](2681-ray-filtering.md)
Ray filtering reduces computational load by discarding rays that do not intersect with the scene's geometry or alpha mask before expensive volume rendering steps. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by operating as a pre-processing culling stage on a batch of rays, often integrating alpha-mask density checks alongside axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersection tests. Choose it when optimizing batch ray processing pipelines [G].

### [Procedural Ray/Box Intersection](8356-procedural-ray-box-intersection.md)
Procedural Ray/Box Intersection determines ray entry and exit within a volume's bounding box entirely within the fragment shader, without pre-rendering geometry. It computes the ray's intersection parameters directly in the shader, allowing the volume to be rendered without rasterized bounding box primitives. It sets itself apart by being self-contained in the shader, placing the full computational load of intersection and marching there instead of using rasterization setup. Choose it when avoiding explicit geometry buffers is required [G].

#### Clipping Cell-Level Slice to Active Rays
An optimization to reduce cell primitives in a slice by intersecting individual rays with the world-space bounding box of the current u,v slice [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart by ignoring rays that have already successfully hit a cell (inactive rays), even if they intersect the slice bounding box [S1, unofficial]. Choose it when optimizing octree-based slice rendering [G].

## Background
Originated in interactive volume rendering research, specifically within octree-based ray tracing pipelines for implicit surfaces [S1, unofficial]. Used to optimize slice rendering by culling empty macrocells and filtering rays against bounding volumes [S1, unofficial].
